title: Service-class windowed admission broker and adaptive overload shedder
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Build a windowed admission broker for Dedicated fleets that enforces service-class throughput guarantees while enabling low-latency admission decisions and adaptive overload shedding. The broker will operate at the routing layer to combine short-term admission control (millisecond token buckets and queue slots) with long-term sliding-window quotas (per service-class and per-tenant) and a coordination channel to autoscaling to create proactive headroom. The goal is to reliably meet per-service throughput SLAs under bursty demand and partial capacity loss, and to degrade predictably and fairly across service classes when unavoidable.
background: Current dedicated fleet behavior uses coarse admission and shedding heuristics that react slowly to sudden bursts and do not coordinate well with autoscaler warm-up. We’ve observed tenant-visible SLO violations during regional capacity churn and during cross-tenant bursts. Existing tickets (referenced in dependencies) implemented priority admission and token reservation primitives, but we need a holistic broker that stitches short and long windows together and provides a predictable degradation model for multi-tenant fleets.
goals: 1) Enforce per-service throughput guarantees expressed as tokens/sec and windowed minimums. 2) Admit requests with low median decision latency (<2ms) using a fast path. 3) Coordinate with autoscaler to request pre-warmed headroom when window exhaustion is imminent. 4) Provide graceful, weighted degradation that preserves high-priority classes and degrades low-priority classes first. 5) Provide observability and test harnesses to validate behavior under synthetic and real traffic.
non_goals: This ticket does not change model-level batching internals or kernel selection logic. It does not implement RBAC or billing changes; per-tenant billing quotas are out of scope.
success_metrics: 1) Median admission decision latency < 2ms on the fast path. 2) 99th percentile request latency increase < 25% during controlled overload tests. 3) Windowed guarantee satisfaction: >=95% of 1-minute windows meet the configured minimum throughput for P0/P1 service-classes. 4) During regional partial outage tests, overall SLA-preserving degradation matches policy in >=90% of trials.
acceptance_criteria: Broker implements short-window token admission (10s sliding token-bucket) and long-window quota tracking (1m and 5m windows) per service-class.
Autoscaler coordination API integrated: broker can emit headroom requests and receive capacity-ready callbacks.
Configurable per-service weights for weighted shedding and explicit rule to protect high-priority classes.
End-to-end integration test that simulates a 3x burst and demonstrates graceful weighted degradation across service-classes with metrics captured to the canary dashboard.
Monitoring dashboards and alerts for bucket exhaustion, headroom requests, and shed events added to console-ops and SRE runbooks.
Performance testing shows admission overhead <2ms median on dedicated routing path and <10% CPU overhead on broker components at 95th percentile load.
design_decision_summary: We chose a hybrid two-tier admission model: a nanosecond-resident fast-path token bucket for immediate admission and a background windowed quota aggregator that periodically reconciles rates and triggers autoscaler actions. For fairness we implement a weighted deficit-round-robin slot allocator across classes when queues form. Shedding is multi-stage: soft-shedding via queue prioritization and delayed responses (grace windows), followed by hard rejects using HTTP 429 when thresholds are crossed. Circuit breakers are tenant-scoped and emit structured events for downstream rollback policies.
architecture: Components: 1) Edge broker instantiated per routing shard, maintains in-memory fast token buckets and per-service short queues. 2) Window aggregator service (eventual-consistent) that stores 1m/5m windows in the fleet time-series store and provides APIs for headroom prediction. 3) Autoscaler coordination channel (gRPC) that accepts headroom requests with priority hints and a desired warmup window. 4) Control plane policy store for per-service-class configs (weights, min-throughput, burst-cap). The edge broker falls back to a conservative admission policy if it loses connectivity to the aggregator.
flow_steps: 1) Request arrives at routing shard; broker performs token check against short-window bucket for the request's service-class.
2) If token present -> admit immediate fast path; emit trace and metric. If token absent -> consult short queue and service weight to decide soft-queueing or immediate rejection.
3) Background aggregator updates long-window usage every 10s; if long-window projected exhaustion < 30s, it signals autoscaler with required headroom and priority.
4) Autoscaler responds when capacity is ready; aggregator and brokers adjust token replenishment rates accordingly.

5) During sustained overload, weighted degradation reduces token rates for lower-priority classes first using configurable slopes; hard rejects start only once soft-queue depths exceed durable thresholds.
implementation_tasks: Edge broker: implement high-performance token bucket with per-shard in-memory counters and lock-free increment path.
Queue allocator: implement weighted slot allocator with fairness guarantees under contention.
Aggregator: implement 10s reconciliation loop, store to time-series (existing metrics store), headroom prediction routine.
Autoscaler API: define and implement headroom request/ack protocol (gRPC), and integration test with existing autoscaler stubs.
Policy UI: add control plane schema for per-service-class weights and windows; wire into console feature flag for canary.
Instrumentation: traces, structured shed events, per-tenant circuit-breaker metrics.
E2E tests: synthetic burst harness, chaos tests for partial shard loss, and canary with subset of customers.
rollout_plan: 1) Feature gated behind dedicated-adv-broker flag. 2) Canary to 2 small dedicated pools with non-critical customers for 48 hours, monitor key metrics. 3) Gradual enablement across fleets with automated rollback criteria (drop in throughput guarantee satisfaction > 10% or error rate spike > 2x baseline). 4) Full rollout after 2 weeks of stable canaries and signoff from SRE and product.
monitoring_and_alerting: Dashboard: broker-admission-latency (p50/p95/p99), token-bucket-utilization by class, queued-requests by class, shed-rate by class.
Alert: sustained 1-minute window satisfaction < 90% for P0 or P1 (page SRE).
Alert: more than 5 manual headroom requests in 10 minutes from a single shard (ops investigation).
Audit log: emit structured events for all hard-shed decisions for downstream post-mortem reproducibility.
testing_plan: Unit tests for token-bucket edge cases (clock drift, negative replenish).
Integration test: broker + aggregator + autoscaler mock verifying headroom lifecycle.
Load test: synthetic traffic replay of production traces with multi-tenant interference to verify fairness heuristics.
Chaos test: kill 1/3 of routing shards and assert degrade behavior matches policy and that autoscaler receives headroom signals.
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: false positives in headroom prediction could cause unnecessary autoscaler churn. Mitigation: conservative smoothing with hysteresis and a backoff policy for repeated requests. Risk: additional CPU on routing shards. Mitigation: implement fast-path in native code path with microbenchmarks and fail open to conservative admission when overloaded.
